passages.t: Melchizedek, king of righteousness and peace
passages.happening:
At last the writer explains the name he has mentioned three times.

“This Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and Abraham apportioned to him a tenth of everything” (verses 1-2).

He explains the names. “First, his name means ‘king of righteousness.’ Then also, ‘king of Salem’ means ‘king of peace.’” (verse 2).

Then he says something surprising. “Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The writer retells a short story from Genesis 14. Abraham had rescued his nephew Lot by defeating a group of kings. On his way home, a king of Salem named Melchizedek came out to meet him. He was also a priest of ‘God Most High’. He blessed Abraham, and Abraham gave him a tenth of what he had won.

Names mattered in the Bible. ‘Melchizedek’ means ‘king of righteousness’, and ‘Salem’, the writer says, means ‘peace’. So he is a king of righteousness and a king of peace. Isaiah had promised a son of David whose rule would bring both: “Of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end” (Isaiah 9:7).

In Israel, a priest had to prove his family line. He had to show that he came from Aaron. Men who could not find their family records were not allowed to serve. A priest with no family tree was unthinkable. Yet Genesis tells of this priest with no father, no mother, no family line, no birth and no death. He simply appears, serves as priest, and is gone.

The writer sees meaning in that silence. Jewish teachers sometimes taught from what a passage leaves out as well as from what it says. As Genesis tells it, Melchizedek stands as a picture of a priest who does not get his office from his family and whose service has no end. In that way he is ‘like the Son of God’.
passages.ot:
The story is in Genesis 14: “Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine—since he was priest of God Most High— and he blessed Abram” (Genesis 14:18-19). His blessing praised “God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth” (Genesis 14:19). “Then Abram gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything” (Genesis 14:20). In its own setting it is the meeting of two men who served the same God: the one God had chosen, Abram, and a king outside his family who knew the Creator too.

Salem is usually identified with Jerusalem. A psalm puts the names together: “His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion” (Psalm 76:2).

Melchizedek is named only once more in the Old Testament, in Psalm 110:4, as the site's notes on Genesis 14 and Psalm 110 explain.

How strict the rule about priestly families was can be seen after the exile, when some men “searched for their family records, but they could not find them and so were excluded from the priesthood” (Ezra 2:62).
passages.hard:
‘Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life.’ Is Hebrews saying Melchizedek had no parents, or that he was more than human?

Most readers take the words as a point about what Genesis leaves unsaid. Genesis usually tells us the family of important people, and sometimes when they were born and when they died. For Melchizedek it tells nothing. He appears in three verses and is gone. On this reading Hebrews does not claim he had no parents. It says that Scripture presents him that way, so that he can stand as a picture of a priest whose office does not come by family and does not end. Notice that he is ‘like the Son of God’: he resembles the Son, not the other way round. This is the reading the site's notes on Genesis 14 and Psalm 110 follow.

Other readings have been held. Some Christians, early and late, have thought Melchizedek was the Son of God himself, appearing before he was born as a man; others reply that ‘like the Son of God’ suggests a different person. Some ancient Jewish teachers said he was Noah's son Shem. A scroll found among the Dead Sea Scrolls pictures him as a heavenly figure who brings release and judgment at the end; but Hebrews has already shown the Son far above the angels.

Whoever Melchizedek was, Genesis says no more than three verses, and it is wise not to say more than it does. What matters for Hebrews is the point he pictures: Jesus is a priest not by family line, but ‘by the power of an indestructible life’ (verse 16).
passages.asks: Melchizedek is a king of righteousness and a king of peace. Ask where you need both, justice and peace, in your life or around you. Ask what it means that your priest's work does not depend on any family line or human system, but on his own life that does not end. And ask where you are tempted to say more than Scripture says.

passages.happening:
“Consider how great Melchizedek was: Even the patriarch Abraham gave him a tenth of the plunder” (verse 4).

The writer explains. The law commanded the priests from Levi's tribe to collect a tenth from their fellow Israelites, who were all descended from Abraham. “But Melchizedek, who did not trace his descent from Levi, collected a tenth from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. And indisputably, the lesser is blessed by the greater” (verses 6-7).

“In the case of the Levites, mortal men collect the tenth; but in the case of Melchizedek, it is affirmed that he lives on” (verse 8).

“And so to speak, Levi, who collects the tenth, paid the tenth through Abraham. For when Melchizedek met Abraham, Levi was still in the loin of his ancestor” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
Abraham was the great father of Israel, the one who ‘had the promises’. Yet he gave a tenth to Melchizedek and received his blessing. In the ancient world, giving a tenth honoured someone as higher, and a blessing was given by the greater to the lesser. So Melchizedek's priesthood stands higher even than Abraham.

The writer then makes a bold step, and he marks it with ‘so to speak’. Levi, the ancestor of Israel's priests, was Abraham's great-grandson. He was not yet born when Abraham met Melchizedek. But people then thought of children as present in their ancestors. So, in a manner of speaking, Levi himself gave a tenth to Melchizedek through Abraham. The priests who receive tithes once paid tithes to a greater priest.

‘He lives on’ points again to the silence of Genesis. It records no death for Melchizedek. The Levitical priests died one after another. The picture points to a priest who lives.

The writer is not making Abraham or Levi small. He calls Abraham ‘the patriarch’ and honours him as the one who received God's promises. He is showing, from Israel's own Scriptures, that God had a priesthood greater still in view.
passages.ot:
The law gave the tithes to the Levites: “Behold, I have given to the Levites all the tithes in Israel as an inheritance in return for the work they do, the service of the Tent of Meeting” (Numbers 18:21). In its setting this was God's provision for the tribe that had no land of its own to farm, because they served at God's tent.

The blessing Melchizedek spoke over Abraham is in Genesis: “Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth” (Genesis 14:19).

The idea of descendants being present in an ancestor runs through Genesis. God told Jacob, “A nation—even a company of nations—shall come from you, and kings shall descend from you” (Genesis 35:11).
passages.hard:
Is the tithe here a rule for Christians today?

Christians answer in different ways, as the site's note on Genesis 14 explains. Some hold that a tenth is still the pattern for God's people, since Abraham gave it before the law of Moses. Others point out that Abraham gave a tenth once, from the spoils of a battle, and that the New Testament does not command a tithe but teaches generous, glad giving: “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). These notes do not settle it.

Hebrews is not teaching about giving here at all. It mentions the tithe only to show that Melchizedek was greater than Abraham.

If you gave money because you were pressed or frightened, or because someone promised that God would pay you back, and the return never came, that was not your failure. You were not lacking in faith. The promise was wrong. It may help to talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If you are in money trouble now, look for a trusted adviser where you live; these notes are not financial advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Even Abraham bowed to receive a blessing. Ask whether you are willing to receive from others, or only to give. Ask what it means that God had a greater priest in view all along, long before the law. And ask whether you hold the great people of faith in honour, while trusting the one greater than them all.

passages.t: A change of priesthood, and a better hope
passages.happening:
Now the writer turns to the psalm. “Now if perfection could have been attained through the Levitical priesthood (for on this basis the people received the law), why was there still need for another priest to appear—one in the order of Melchizedek and not in the order of Aaron?” (verse 11).

“For when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed as well” (verse 12). Jesus came from the tribe of Judah, “a tribe as to which Moses said nothing about priests” (verse 14). He became a priest “not by a law of succession, but by the power of an indestructible life. For it is testified: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’” (verses 16-17).

“So the former commandment is set aside because it was weak and useless (for the law made nothing perfect), and a better hope is introduced, by which we draw near to God” (verses 18-19).
passages.hearers:
The argument depends on timing. Psalm 110 was spoken long after Moses and Aaron. If Aaron's priesthood was God's final word, why would God speak, centuries later, of a different priest, ‘in the order of Melchizedek’? The psalm itself shows that God had more in mind.

‘Perfection’ in Hebrews means reaching the goal: people brought fully to God, with consciences made clean. The writer says the Levitical priesthood could not do that by itself. That was never its job.

‘The law must be changed as well.’ The law and the priesthood went together. The rule that priests must come from Levi was part of the law. If God names a priest from another order, then that rule no longer governs who is priest.

Jesus was from Judah, the tribe of the kings. Moses never spoke of priests from Judah. So Jesus is not a priest by the old rule of family. He is a priest ‘by the power of an indestructible life’. He died, but death could not hold him, and he lives forever.

‘The former commandment’ is the rule about priestly descent. It is ‘set aside’, a word used for cancelling a legal document. ‘Weak and useless’ is strong language. But notice what it is weak for: it could not make anyone ‘perfect’, could not bring people all the way to God. And notice where the writer ends: ‘a better hope is introduced, by which we draw near to God.’
passages.ot:
Verse 17 quotes Psalm 110:4 again: “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” In its own setting, as the site's note on Psalm 110 explains, God gives a king of David's line a priestly role, which would have surprised an Israelite, since kings and priests were kept apart.

The law itself was God's good gift, and the Old Testament loves it: “The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul” (Psalm 19:7). Paul says, “So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good” (Romans 7:12).

Yet the same Paul speaks of what the law could not do: “For what the law was powerless to do in that it was weakened by the flesh, God did by sending His own Son” (Romans 8:3). The weakness lay not in God's law but in what it was given to do, and in the people it was given to.

Judah was the tribe of kings: “The scepter will not depart from Judah” (Genesis 49:10).
passages.hard:
‘Weak and useless.’ Is Hebrews saying the law of Moses was bad, or that Jewish worship was worthless?

No. Read it closely. ‘The former commandment’ here is the rule that priests must come from Levi's family. It is called weak and useless for one purpose: it could not make anyone ‘perfect’, that is, bring people all the way to God with cleansed consciences. It was never meant to. It served a real purpose for its time, and Hebrews itself says the priesthood was given by God (5:4).

The Bible calls God's law ‘perfect’ (Psalm 19:7) and ‘holy, righteous, and good’ (Romans 7:12). Paul says its weakness came from human sin, not from the law (Romans 8:3). Hebrews is arguing from Israel's own Scriptures, Psalm 110 above all, that God had always planned a priest greater than Aaron.

For centuries some Christians used this letter, with other parts of the New Testament, to teach contempt for Jews and Judaism. That reading is false. This site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why, and the book page's part on the old covenant and the Jewish people says more.

Christians also differ on how the law of Moses still guides believers. Many hold that its moral commands still show God's will, while its rules for priests and sacrifices are fulfilled in Christ. Others hold that the whole law reached its goal in Christ, and that believers now live ‘under the law of Christ’ (1 Corinthians 9:21). The doctrine study ‘The Law’ sets out these views and others. These notes do not choose.
passages.asks: ‘A better hope, by which we draw near to God.’ Ask whether your hope rests on anything you do or inherit, or on Christ's life that cannot be destroyed. Ask how you speak about the law and about the Jewish people, and whether it is with honour. And ask what it would mean today to ‘draw near to God’.

passages.t: A priest forever who always lives to intercede
passages.happening:
“And none of this happened without an oath. For others became priests without an oath, but Jesus became a priest with an oath by the One who said to Him: ‘The Lord has sworn and will not change His mind: ‘You are a priest forever.’’ Because of this oath, Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant” (verses 20-22).

“Now there have been many other priests, since death prevented them from continuing in office. But because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood. Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them” (verses 23-25).

“Such a high priest truly befits us—One who is holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. Unlike the other high priests, He does not need to offer daily sacrifices, first for His own sins and then for the sins of the people; He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself” (verses 26-27).

“For the law appoints as high priests men who are weak; but the oath, which came after the law, appointed the Son, who has been made perfect forever” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The writer makes three last comparisons.

First, the oath. Israel's priests took office by family, with no oath from God. Jesus was made priest by God's oath, the oath in Psalm 110:4. Because of it he is ‘the guarantee of a better covenant’. A guarantee was a legal word for someone who pledged himself to make good on a promise. The word ‘covenant’ appears here for the first time in the letter, and it will fill the next three chapters.

Second, life. Israel had many priests over the centuries, because each one died and another took his place. Jesus has one priesthood that never passes to anyone else, because he lives forever. So he can ‘save completely’, all the way and for all time, everyone who comes to God through him. He ‘always lives to intercede’, to speak to God on their behalf. His work for his people did not end at the cross. It goes on.

Third, the sacrifice. Israel's high priests had to offer sacrifices for their own sins first. Jesus did not. He is ‘holy, innocent, undefiled’. And he offered not an animal but himself, ‘once for all’. Here, for the first time, the letter says plainly that the priest and the sacrifice are the same person.
passages.ot:
Verse 21 quotes the first half of Psalm 110:4 for the first time: “The LORD has sworn and will not change His mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek’” (Psalm 110:4). An oath from God was the strongest promise the Bible knows.

The high priest's order of sacrifice, first for himself and then for the people, comes from the Day of Atonement: “Aaron is to present the bull for his sin offering and make atonement for himself and his household” (Leviticus 16:6), and then he “shall then slaughter the goat for the sin offering for the people” (Leviticus 16:15).

The servant of the LORD in Isaiah both gave himself and prayed for others: “because He has poured out His life unto death, and He was numbered with the transgressors. Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12).
passages.hard:
‘Made perfect forever’ (verse 28). Was the Son once imperfect?

No. As in 2:10 and 5:9, ‘made perfect’ in Hebrews means made complete for his work. The same verse calls him ‘the Son’, and verse 26 calls him ‘holy, innocent, undefiled’. Through his obedience, death and rising, he was installed as the high priest his people need, and he remains so forever. The church confesses him as ‘truly God and truly man’, ‘in all things like unto us, without sin’, in the words of the Council of Chalcedon.

And what of ‘He always lives to intercede’? Does Jesus have to persuade an unwilling Father? No. The Father himself appointed this priest by oath, because he wants his people saved. Christ's prayer for his people is the Father's own will, carried out by the Son who knows our weakness. It is one of the most comforting words in the Bible: someone is praying for you who never stops and never fails.
passages.asks: He is able to save completely, and he always lives to intercede. Ask what part of your life you think is too far gone to be saved completely. Ask what it means that Jesus is praying for you now. And ask whether you are coming to God through him, or trying to come some other way.
